reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: The commonest site of injury is the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus, producing wrist drop, finger drop and weak thumb extension with sensory loss over the dorsal first web space

The classic compressive 'Saturday night palsy' follows prolonged external pressure on the arm, often with sleep after alcohol; humeral shaft fracture (notably the Holstein-Lewis distal-third fracture) is a key traumatic cause

A spiral-groove lesion spares triceps and the elbow-extension reflex because branches to triceps arise proximally, whereas a very proximal axillary lesion (for example crutch palsy) also weakens triceps

Brachioradialis and supinator weakness helps localise a lesion at or above the elbow, and the radially deviated posture on attempted wrist extension reflects preserved extensor carpi radialis longus with weak extensor carpi ulnaris
Finger drop with preserved wrist extension and no sensory loss indicates a posterior interosseous (deep motor branch) lesion rather than a main radial trunk palsy
Apparent hand-grip weakness is often spurious, resulting from loss of wrist extension that shortens the finger flexors; grip normalises when the wrist is passively supported

Most neuropraxic and compressive lesions recover spontaneously; a cock-up wrist splint maintains function, and tendon transfers are considered when there is no recovery after adequate time and electrophysiological follow-up
reference.pathophysiology: The radial nerve, the terminal continuation of the posterior cord (C5-T1), descends through the axilla, winds around the humerus in the spiral groove between the heads of triceps, then pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to reach the anterior compartment at the elbow, where it divides into the superficial (sensory) radial nerve and the posterior interosseous (deep motor) branch. Its close apposition to the humerus in the spiral groove and its tethering at the lateral intermuscular septum render it susceptible to external compression, fracture and traction. Compression typically produces focal demyelination with conduction block and good prognosis, whereas transection or severe traction causes axonal loss requiring regeneration over months; the motor deficit reflects paralysis of the wrist, finger and thumb extensors and, in proximal lesions, the elbow extensors.
additionalDifferentials: Posterior interosseous nerve syndrome (finger drop without wrist drop or sensory loss)
Central lesion causing pseudo-radial upper-limb weakness (cortical hand knob stroke)
Lead neuropathy causing bilateral wrist drop
Extensor tendon rupture at the wrist
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies to localise the lesion and identify conduction block at the spiral groove
Needle electromyography sampling triceps, brachioradialis, extensor and forearm muscles to define the level and axonal loss
Plain radiographs of the humerus if fracture or callus entrapment is suspected
High-resolution ultrasound or MRI neurography to demonstrate focal nerve enlargement, mass or entrapment
Serum lead concentration when bilateral wrist drop is present
Cervical spine imaging if radiculopathy is a competing diagnosis
redFlags: Wrist drop developing acutely after humeral fracture or fracture manipulation, suggesting nerve entrapment or laceration
Bilateral wrist drop raising concern for lead toxicity or a systemic neuropathy
Rapidly progressive or painful onset suggesting inflammatory neuralgic amyotrophy or vasculitis
Associated triceps weakness and axillary sensory loss indicating a proximal plexus or cord lesion
reference.prognosis: Compressive and neuropraxic palsies usually recover fully over weeks to a few months once conduction block resolves. Lesions with significant axonal loss recover more slowly and incompletely, and those associated with nerve transection require surgical repair with a more guarded outcome.
pitfalls: Interpreting grip weakness as median or ulnar dysfunction when it is secondary to loss of wrist extension
Missing a posterior interosseous lesion by not testing for preserved wrist extension and intact sensation
Failing to recognise triceps sparing as evidence for a spiral-groove rather than axillary lesion
Overlooking a humeral fracture or delayed entrapment in callus as the cause
Not considering neuralgic amyotrophy or lead toxicity in atypical, painful or bilateral presentations
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Removal of the source of external compression in neuropraxic 'Saturday night' palsy and reduction and stabilisation of any humeral shaft fracture causing the lesion
A cock-up wrist splint with dynamic finger-extension outriggers to prevent contractures and maintain hand function during recovery
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy to preserve joint range and retrain wrist and finger extension
Watchful waiting for compressive and neuropraxic lesions, which usually recover once conduction block resolves
Serial nerve conduction studies and electromyography to track reinnervation and detect axonal-loss lesions that fail to recover
Surgical exploration with nerve repair or grafting, and tendon transfers as a salvage option, when transection or severe traction prevents recovery
